source.title: Understanding Scaling Laws for Recommendation Models
source.authors: Newsha Ardalani; Carole-Jean Wu; Zeliang Chen; Bhargav Bhushanam; Adnan Aziz

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, including appendices. Some figure and table text is flattened or garbled in extraction; the paper is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling relationships in production-scale recommendation models, a domain beyond language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling results for recommendation models. It also cites language-model scaling results, which are not recorded as this study's results. Its fixed-compute comparisons are recorded as findings but do not establish a stable compute-optimal parameter/data trend.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own power-law-plus-constant curves of held-out normalized test loss against data, parameters and compute for a production DLRM-style CTR recommendation model. This is a new domain beyond text pretraining, so it bears on V5. It does not train language models, so V1–V4, V6 and V7, which are stated for language-model pretraining, are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors add that the irreducible constant is bounded near 0.98 normalized entropy. They also say future hardware should be designed for larger datasets rather than larger models.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes DLRM-style CTR models, using normalized cross-entropy loss after one epoch and power-law-plus-constant fits; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling efficiency differs by resource axis and scaling scheme. The training-data and test-data loss curves have different exponents. The preferred parameter-scaling scheme depends on data and parameter budget.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute, larger datasets give lower loss and larger models give worse loss. A Pareto line of best model size per compute is drawn, but no allocation exponent is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In one-epoch CTR recommendation models, compute is better spent on data than on parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: The best parameter-scaling scheme (vertical vs horizontal embedding; overarch vs MLP) depends on the data and parameter budget regime (Figs 7–8, Table 2). The optimal embedding dimension shrinks as table rows grow, with the knee near 64 (Fig 9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In recommendation models, the effect of architectural shape on loss depends on the data/parameter regime.

record.problems: The analysis uses one production-level recommendation model and one-epoch training. Compute is varied indirectly through dataset size and/or model size; longer training is left for future work. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates. Some figure/table text is flattened in the supplied extraction.

untested.parts: Image/video modalities, repeated-data (multi-epoch) training, fine-tuning and transfer. All runs are one epoch, and compute scaling by longer training is left for future work.
All parts: no extrapolation from small fits to much larger runs is tested, even in the recommendation setting.
All parts for language models. In recommendation models the study reports fixed-compute comparisons and a Pareto line, but no fitted allocation exponents.

missing.what: Per-scheme exponents. Data scaling (Fig 4): vertical 0.12, horizontal 0.10, overarch 0.10, MLP 0.09. Compute scaling (Fig 5): horizontal 0.12, overarch 0.14, MLP 0.15.
Parameter-scaling goodness of fit R2=0.9 and the saturated flag
Statement, without data shown, that input granularity/vocabulary size has no significant impact on the scaling trend

record.verdict_notes: This is a single production model on a proprietary dataset. Loss is normalized to the minimum observed NE. No uncertainty is reported, and there is no held-out extrapolation test. Parameter counts exclude embeddings for the MLP and overarch schemes only. Table 1's flattened columns make the α/β assignment for parameter scaling ambiguous.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small runs predict much larger language-model runs.

A stable power-of-compute trend in the loss-minimising parameter and token counts; the study compares recommendation-model choices at fixed compute but does not fit optimal allocations across compute budgets.
Whether architecture details have little effect on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
The study tests CTR recommendation models, not image/video modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream task performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with fitting/setup choices, or curves bend away from a single power law.

5M to 5120M samples are listed in the methodology; exact points per fit not stated

rows.measure: Normalized test loss versus dataset size; power-law-plus-constant fit, L(x)=αx^-β+γ.
rows.note: Aggregate ranges are those reported across scaling schemes; no per-scheme values are assigned from flattened figure labels.
rows.check: Values are from Pareto-frontier fits. Loss is normalized to the minimum observed NE and spans only about 1.00–1.04, so the fitted range is narrow. Data spans 5M–5120M samples, about three orders of magnitude.

source_check.correct: The reported coefficients describe Pareto-frontier fits across model sizes, not individual fixed-model-size curves. Table 1 reports α=0.07, β=[0.09,0.12], γ=[0.97,0.98], R²=0.999.
source_check.locator_found: Section 2.1; Figure 4 caption; Table 1; Appendix A.4.
source_check.problem: The operation conflates fixed-model-size experimental curves with the Pareto-frontier curves supplying the coefficients.

rows.subject: production-level recommendation model (DLRM-style; exact model name not stated)
rows.size_stated: Parameter scaling schemes vary model size; exact sizes not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Scaled parameter count using vertical and horizontal embedding, overarch-layer, or MLP-layer scaling.

conditions.value: vertical embedding, horizontal embedding, overarch, and MLP scaling

rows.measure: Normalized test loss versus parameter count; fitted power-law-plus-constant relationship and saturation.
rows.value: Parameter-scaling α ranges from 0.4 to 7.6; the paper says all schemes operate in the saturating phase and that parameter scaling has weak or negligible impact at industry scale. Table 1 reports γ=[0.97-1].
rows.note: The text gives α and saturation explicitly. The flattened Table 1 does not support a reliable assignment of all remaining fit coefficients.
rows.check: Value is incomplete. Table 1 gives parameter-scaling fit R2=0.9 (vs 0.999 for data and compute) and marks the curve saturated. Column alignment in the flattened Table 1 is ambiguous: the [0.4–7.6] range sits in the β column while the text calls it α, so the coefficient assignment is uncertain. Partial is right: a fit exists, but loss depends only weakly on parameters and the paper says parameter scaling plays a 'negligible role'.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V5's power-law form. The authors report a saturated power-law-plus-constant parameter fit with R²=0.9. Section 1.1 calls [0.4,7.6] α, whereas Table 1 places that range under β and gives α=(0,0.5].
source_check.locator_found: Section 1.1, Parameter Scaling Efficiency; Table 1; Section 2.3; Figure 6.
source_check.problem: Weak marginal parameter gains do not establish an incomplete power-law form; the coefficient attribution also contains an inconsistency in the paper.

rows.operation_detail: Compared data-scaling learning curves evaluated on training data and test data.
rows.measure: Power-law exponent for data-scaling loss curves.
rows.value: The paper reports a steeper training-data curve (-0.20) than the test-data curve (-0.12).
rows.note: The reported difference is between evaluation sets for the same model trained on the same data.
rows.check: Only the test-loss curve is held-out loss, and it duplicates the data-scaling fit in R1 (β≈0.12). The training-loss exponent (-0.20, γ 0.99) is not held-out loss. The row's main content is a difference between evaluation sets, which adds little to V5.

relationships.reason: Normalized test loss fits power law plus constant with R2=0.999: data β 0.09–0.12 (R1), compute β 0.12–0.15 (R3); the test-loss curve in R6 agrees.
relationships.display_finding: Power laws plus constants fit normalized test loss with R² = 0.999, data exponents of 0.09–0.12, and compute exponents of 0.12–0.15.
